sentence: There is ___ milk left, so you can have some in your coffee.
setupText: Choose the phrase that presents a small amount as available and useful.
taskText: There is ___ milk left, so you can have some in your coffee.
text: Choose the phrase that presents a small amount as available and useful. There is ___ milk left, so you can have some in your coffee.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-a2-1101:Positive a little with a mass noun
explanation: A little means a small amount and draws attention to what is available.

rationales.little: Little emphasizes how small the supply is; the requested meaning emphasizes that some is available.
rationales.a little: A little means a small amount and draws attention to what is available.
rationales.a few: A few goes with plural countable things, such as cartons, not milk here.
rationales.no: No milk would leave none to put in the coffee.

sentence: ___ neighbors helped us carry the sofa upstairs.
setupText: Choose a grammatical expression for a number of people, without giving an exact number.
taskText: ___ neighbors helped us carry the sofa upstairs.
text: Choose a grammatical expression for a number of people, without giving an exact number. ___ neighbors helped us carry the sofa upstairs.
explanation: Several indicates a number of people without specifying exactly how many.

rationales.Three: Three is grammatical, but it states an exact number, which the task excludes.
rationales.Much: Much cannot go before the plural countable noun neighbors.
rationales.Several: Several indicates a number of people without specifying exactly how many.
rationales.Each: Each requires a singular noun: each neighbor.

sentence: Please bring ___ ID card to the housing office.
setupText: Choose the form that completes this instruction in standard written English.
taskText: Please bring ___ ID card to the housing office.
text: Choose the form that completes this instruction in standard written English. Please bring ___ ID card to the housing office.
explanation: Your goes before ID card to show that the card belongs to the person being addressed.

rationales.you: You names the person directly; it does not show whose ID card to bring.
rationales.yours: Yours can stand alone, as in Bring yours, but cannot introduce ID card.
rationales.yourself: Yourself refers to you as a person, not to a possession before a noun.
rationales.your: Your goes before ID card to show that the card belongs to the person being addressed.

sentence: Twelve guests need seats, but the room has eight chairs. There are ___.
setupText: Choose the phrase that describes the shortage.
taskText: Twelve guests need seats, but the room has eight chairs. There are ___.
text: Choose the phrase that describes the shortage. Twelve guests need seats, but the room has eight chairs. There are ___.
explanation: Not enough means fewer than needed; eight chairs cannot seat twelve guests.

rationales.not enough chairs: Not enough means fewer than needed; eight chairs cannot seat twelve guests.
rationales.too many chairs: Too many means more than needed; here the room needs four more.
rationales.no chairs: There are eight chairs, so saying no chairs would be inaccurate.
rationales.enough chairs: Enough would provide a seat for every guest, but four guests lack seats.

sentence: This cup is dirty. Could I have ___ cup, please?
setupText: Choose the word for one more cup; no particular cup is meant.
taskText: This cup is dirty. Could I have ___ cup, please?
text: Choose the word for one more cup; no particular cup is meant. This cup is dirty. Could I have ___ cup, please?
explanation: Another means one more or a different one, without identifying a particular cup.

rationales.the other: The other identifies a particular remaining cup in a known pair; no such pair is given.
rationales.another: Another means one more or a different one, without identifying a particular cup.
rationales.other: Before singular cup, use another or a phrase such as the other, not other alone.
rationales.others: Others stands for plural things and does not go directly before cup.

sentence: I know ___ people in this town, so I have someone to ask for help.
setupText: Choose the phrase that emphasizes having a small number available.
taskText: I know ___ people in this town, so I have someone to ask for help.
text: Choose the phrase that emphasizes having a small number available. I know ___ people in this town, so I have someone to ask for help.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-a2-1106:A few for a useful small number
explanation: A few means a small number and presents those contacts as available.

rationales.few: Few emphasizes the smallness of the number, rather than the positive availability requested here.
rationales.a little: A little describes an uncountable amount; people is plural and countable.
rationales.a few: A few means a small number and presents those contacts as available.
rationales.no: No people would not support having someone local to ask.

sentence: My partner and I work from home. ___ use the same desk at different times.
setupText: Choose the phrase that makes a grammatical sentence.
taskText: My partner and I work from home. ___ use the same desk at different times.
text: Choose the phrase that makes a grammatical sentence. My partner and I work from home. ___ use the same desk at different times.
explanation: Both of us refers to the two speakers together and uses us after of.

rationales.Both we: Before the pronoun us, use both of us; both we does not work here.
rationales.Both of we: Of takes the object form us, not the subject form we.
rationales.Both us: Use We both or Both of us as the subject, not Both us.
rationales.Both of us: Both of us refers to the two speakers together and uses us after of.

sentence: I asked two hotels for a room. One was full and the other was full too. ___ hotel had a room for me.
setupText: Choose the word that matches the two answers.
taskText: I asked two hotels for a room. One was full and the other was full too. ___ hotel had a room for me.
text: Choose the word that matches the two answers. I asked two hotels for a room. One was full and the other was full too. ___ hotel had a room for me.
explanation: Neither means not one and not the other, matching the two full hotels.

rationales.Neither: Neither means not one and not the other, matching the two full hotels.
rationales.Either: Either would indicate that one or the other had a room, contrary to both replies.
rationales.Each: Each hotel had a room would say that rooms were available at both hotels.
rationales.One: One hotel had a room would mean a room was available at one of them.

sentence: I am free on Tuesday and Thursday. You can choose ___ day for our call.
setupText: Choose the word that allows a choice of one of two days.
taskText: I am free on Tuesday and Thursday. You can choose ___ day for our call.
text: Choose the word that allows a choice of one of two days. I am free on Tuesday and Thursday. You can choose ___ day for our call.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-a2-1109:Either as one of two available choices
explanation: Either allows you to choose one or the other of the two available days.

rationales.neither: Neither would rule out both days, but both are available.
rationales.either: Either allows you to choose one or the other of the two available days.
rationales.both: Both requires plural days and would select two days, not one.
rationales.every: Every day extends the choice beyond the two named days.

sentence: Please check that ___ the windows are closed before you leave.
setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence.
taskText: Please check that ___ the windows are closed before you leave.
text: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence. Please check that ___ the windows are closed before you leave.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-a2-1110:All before the plus a plural noun
explanation: All the windows includes the complete group of windows and keeps the plural form.

rationales.every: Every needs a singular noun without the: every window.
rationales.whole: Whole cannot directly quantify the plural phrase the windows this way.
rationales.all: All the windows includes the complete group of windows and keeps the plural form.
rationales.each: Each needs a singular noun, or each of the windows; each the windows is incorrect.

sentence: The repair took ___.
setupText: Choose the phrase that means the entire day, from morning until evening.
taskText: The repair took ___.
text: Choose the phrase that means the entire day, from morning until evening. The repair took ___.
explanation: The whole day treats one day as a complete period.

rationales.a few hours: A few hours describes only part of the stated morning-to-evening period.
rationales.every day: Every day describes repetition across days, not the length of one repair.
rationales.half the day: Half the day covers only part of the full day in the task.
rationales.the whole day: The whole day treats one day as a complete period.

sentence: Eight of the ten team members cycle to work. ___ cycle to work.
setupText: Choose the phrase meaning more than half, without stating the exact number.
taskText: Eight of the ten team members cycle to work. ___ cycle to work.
text: Choose the phrase meaning more than half, without stating the exact number. Eight of the ten team members cycle to work. ___ cycle to work.
explanation: Most of them means more than half of this known group, matching eight out of ten.

rationales.Most of them: Most of them means more than half of this known group, matching eight out of ten.
rationales.Half of them: Half of ten is five; eight is more than half.
rationales.All of them: All would include ten people, but two do not cycle.
rationales.None of them: None would mean zero cyclists, contrary to the eight stated.

sentence: ___ apples in this bag are damaged.
setupText: Choose the words that make a grammatical sentence.
taskText: ___ apples in this bag are damaged.
text: Choose the words that make a grammatical sentence. ___ apples in this bag are damaged.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-a2-1113:Some of the plus a plural noun
explanation: Some of the apples selects an unspecified part of the identified bagful.

rationales.Some of: After some of, a noun group needs a word such as the: some of the apples.
rationales.Some of the: Some of the apples selects an unspecified part of the identified bagful.
rationales.Some the: Some the omits the of needed between some and the apples.
rationales.Some of this: This is singular, but apples is plural; use these or the after of.

sentence: How many spare batteries do we have? We have ___.
setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical answer meaning zero.
taskText: How many spare batteries do we have? We have ___.
text: Choose the word that makes a grammatical answer meaning zero. How many spare batteries do we have? We have ___.
explanation: None can stand alone and means zero batteries in this answer.

rationales.no: No needs a noun here: no spare batteries. It cannot complete We have by itself.
rationales.neither: Neither refers to two specified alternatives, not an unspecified stock of batteries.
rationales.none: None can stand alone and means zero batteries in this answer.
rationales.any: We have any does not state zero; use We do not have any or We have none.

sentence: This soup is very salty. I put ___ salt in it.
setupText: Choose the phrase that says the amount is more than wanted.
taskText: This soup is very salty. I put ___ salt in it.
text: Choose the phrase that says the amount is more than wanted. This soup is very salty. I put ___ salt in it.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-a2-1115:Too much for an excessive mass quantity
explanation: Too much salt means more salt than wanted, explaining the unpleasant taste.

rationales.a little: A little describes a small amount without saying it was excessive.
rationales.not enough: Not enough says more was needed, the opposite of the stated problem.
rationales.too many: Many cannot quantify the uncountable noun salt here.
rationales.too much: Too much salt means more salt than wanted, explaining the unpleasant taste.

sentence: I have ___ meetings today; I cannot finish my other work.
setupText: Choose the phrase that says the number is more than the speaker can manage.
taskText: I have ___ meetings today; I cannot finish my other work.
text: Choose the phrase that says the number is more than the speaker can manage. I have ___ meetings today; I cannot finish my other work.
explanation: Too many meetings means the number causes a problem, here leaving too little work time.

rationales.too many: Too many meetings means the number causes a problem, here leaving too little work time.
rationales.too much: Much does not fit the plural countable noun meetings.
rationales.a few: A few gives a small number without expressing the excess required by the task.
rationales.no: No meetings would leave no meeting-related reason for the stated difficulty.

sentence: Maya gave me ___ about my first day at work.
setupText: Choose the phrase that makes a grammatical sentence.
taskText: Maya gave me ___ about my first day at work.
text: Choose the phrase that makes a grammatical sentence. Maya gave me ___ about my first day at work.
explanation: Some can introduce uncountable advice, even when useful comes between them.

rationales.a useful advice: Advice is uncountable in this meaning. For one suggestion, say a useful piece of advice.
rationales.some useful advice: Some can introduce uncountable advice, even when useful comes between them.
rationales.a few useful advice: A few needs plural countable things: a few useful suggestions.
rationales.many useful advice: Many needs a plural countable noun; use much advice or many suggestions.

sentence: Some guests are eating inside; ___ guests are eating on the terrace.
setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence.
taskText: Some guests are eating inside; ___ guests are eating on the terrace.
text: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence. Some guests are eating inside; ___ guests are eating on the terrace.
explanation: Other goes before a plural noun to refer to additional or different members of a group.

rationales.another: Another normally introduces one singular guest; guests is plural here.
rationales.others: Others replaces a plural noun; it cannot go directly before guests.
rationales.other: Other goes before a plural noun to refer to additional or different members of a group.
rationales.an other: Before plural guests, use other without an; the article an is singular.

sentence: This building has two lifts. One is broken, but ___ lift works.
setupText: Choose the phrase that identifies the remaining lift in a known pair.
taskText: This building has two lifts. One is broken, but ___ lift works.
text: Choose the phrase that identifies the remaining lift in a known pair. This building has two lifts. One is broken, but ___ lift works.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-a2-1119:The other for the remaining member of a pair
explanation: The other identifies the second and remaining lift after one of two has been mentioned.

rationales.others: Others is a standalone plural form and cannot introduce lift.
rationales.other: Singular lift needs a determiner; other lift alone is incomplete.
rationales.another: Another can introduce a different lift, but does not explicitly identify the remaining member of this pair.
rationales.the other: The other identifies the second and remaining lift after one of two has been mentioned.

sentence: The guests have arrived, but ___ luggage is still at the airport.
setupText: Choose the possessive form used before 'luggage' in standard written English.
taskText: The guests have arrived, but ___ luggage is still at the airport.
text: Choose the possessive form used before 'luggage' in standard written English. The guests have arrived, but ___ luggage is still at the airport.
explanation: 'Their' goes before 'luggage' to show that it belongs to the guests.

rationales.their: 'Their' goes before 'luggage' to show that it belongs to the guests.
rationales.theirs: 'Theirs' stands alone, as in 'The luggage is theirs'; it cannot introduce 'luggage'.
rationales.them: 'Them' is an object form and cannot show possession before 'luggage'.
rationales.they: 'They' is a subject form; the possessive phrase needed here is 'their luggage'.
